# Environment
 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family and Haiku 4.5. Model IDs — Fable 5.1: 'claude-fable-5-1', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5: 'claude-sonnet-5', Haiku 4.5: 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).
 - Fast mode for Claude Code uses Claude Opus with faster output (it does not downgrade to a smaller model). It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

# Finishing work
Ending your turn means your work stops there until asked to continue, and you should not stop unless needed. Please avoid stopping while work the user asked for is still owed. Status notes are welcome, and so are your recommendations on open decisions, but do not stop unnecessarily and carry on with whatever does not depend on the user's answer. If you notice yourself inviting the user to redirect you or offering to wait, instead proceed on the next part of the task. You may meet ordinary obstacles like errors, timeouts, locked files, empty results or failing tools. Diagnose them first, and when they are not real blockers, work through them with the access you have (wait and retry, fix the request, use another tool or source) rather than stopping or checking in. Stopping before the task is complete can rarely be merited, i.e. when the task can't move forward without user input, or where the blocker is deliberate and should not be worked past. This does not override the need for confirmation on risky or destructive actions.

The Edit tool's description says you must Read a file before editing it. That no longer holds for files inside the working directory: Edit works there without a prior Read. When you already know the exact text to replace, for example from grep or cat output, edit directly.

This adds to the Memory section and takes precedence over it. The rules about saving apply only if this session has a directory for saving memories.

Save only what is applicable and durable:
applicable: it would directly change your behavior in future sessions, such as an approach the user corrected or steered you away from, or a standing preference they expressed. Not ambient code context or state.

Avoid saving an unnecessary record of completed work (commits, merges, review outcomes, status summaries). Pointers to external resources and environment facts the user would otherwise have to restate are still worth saving.

Don't overindex on soft feedback - give it the appropriate weight based on the context, and if you can't tell whether it's an instruction or just a comment, ask once but carry on. When saving feedback, record the specifics (what, who, when, why, scope) and label your own interpretations as yours.

Same for your notes - if they contain some caution or limitation, question whether the reason still holds and drop it if not. This isn't a reason to take risky, irreversible, destructive actions without confirmation though, and an old or general go-ahead doesn't count as confirmation, so if the caution is about these kinds of actions then keep it until a human gives confirmation (even if you wrote it yourself).

Don't create planning, decision, or analysis documents unless the user asks for them — work from the context, not intermediate files.

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your one lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Dailies Core Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** From a repository URL, produce a fact-checked, narrated MP4 reel of its recorded coding-agent sessions through a resumable pipeline and a CLI.

**Architecture:** A pnpm TypeScript monorepo. `packages/core` holds every shared schema; each other package exposes plain functions over those schemas. A durable runner executes stages in order and persists each stage's artifact so a run can resume.

**Tech Stack:** Node 22+, pnpm workspaces, TypeScript (strict, ESM), zod, vitest, OpenAI SDK against an OpenAI-compatible gateway, neatlogs SDK, Remotion 4, better-sqlite3, ffmpeg, git, Entire CLI.

**Spec:** `docs/specs/2026-10-11-dailies-design.md`

This plan covers Tier 1 of the spec. The web app, evaluation harness, runtime read-back and deployment are separate plans that build on the interfaces fixed here.

## Global Constraints

- Node `>=22`. TypeScript `strict: true`, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"`.
- Internal packages are consumed as TypeScript source: `"exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" }`. No build step; run with `tsx`, check with `tsc --noEmit`.
- Package names: `@dailies/core`, `@dailies/ingest`, `@dailies/agent`, `@dailies/verify`, `@dailies/voice`, `@dailies/reel`, `@dailies/pipeline`, `@dailies/cli`.
- A package imports another only through its index. Shared types live in `@dailies/core` and nowhere else.
- A task edits files only inside the directories listed under its **Files**. Do not change another package's `package.json`.
- Tests: vitest, files `packages/<name>/test/*.test.ts`. Run one package with `pnpm --filter @dailies/<name> test`.
- No secret ever enters the repository. Configuration comes from `.env` through `loadEnv()`.
- Every model call goes through `@dailies/agent`. No other package imports `openai`.
- Model ids on the gateway: `claude-sonnet-4.6`, `claude-haiku`, `nova-pro`. Gateway base URL: `LITELLM_BASE_URL`. Stay under 50 requests per minute.
- Trace endpoint: `https://ingest.neatlogs.com`.
- A verdict is `verified` only on positive evidence. Anything unknown is `unverifiable`, never `verified` and never `contradicted`.
- Commit after every green test cycle with a short imperative message.
- Once code exists, locate it with `entire graph search` before broad grep, as `CLAUDE.md` instructs.

## Review Focus

1. A repository with no checkpoints, or none inside the window: the run ends early with a clear message and no render. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 10.
2. A tool result of several megabytes or with ANSI colour codes: entries are truncated head-and-tail, colour codes are stripped, memory stays flat. Pinned in Task 2 and Task 4.
3. A claim quote that differs from the transcript only by whitespace or Markdown marks: still matched. A quote that is not in the entry: dropped. Pinned in Task 4.
4. A test run whose output the parser does not recognise: `unknown`, so the claim is `unverifiable`. Pinned in Task 4.
5. Narration audio whose pause count does not equal the line count: timings fall back to proportional alignment and never throw. Pinned in Task 5.
6. A model reply that is not valid JSON for the schema: one repair turn, then the stage fails and the runner retries it. Pinned in Task 3.
7. A secret inside a human prompt or a tool result: redacted at ingest, before any model or renderer sees it. Pinned in Task 1 and Task 2.

## File Structure

```
package.json  pnpm-workspace.yaml  tsconfig.base.json  vitest.config.ts  .nvmrc
packages/core/src/      schema.ts ids.ts redact.ts env.ts budget.ts facts.ts index.ts
packages/ingest/src/    git.ts checkpoints.ts transcript.ts trailers.ts window.ts index.ts
packages/agent/src/     router.ts meter.ts limiter.ts loop.ts tools.ts trace.ts mock.ts index.ts
packages/verify/src/    commands.ts results.ts rules.ts quote.ts ground.ts style.ts index.ts
packages/voice/src/     gemini.ts wav.ts silence.ts align.ts index.ts
packages/reel/src/      timeline.ts srt.ts theme.ts render.ts index.ts
packages/reel/src/remotion/   index.ts Root.tsx Reel.tsx scenes/*.tsx
packages/pipeline/src/  db.ts store.ts runner.ts types.ts index.ts
packages/pipeline/src/stages/   ingest.ts edit.ts verify.ts script.ts ground.ts voice.ts render.ts review.ts gate.ts
packages/pipeline/src/prompts/  editor.ts extractor.ts judge.ts writer.ts entail.ts reviewer.ts
packages/cli/src/       index.ts run.ts verify.ts
packages/cli/bin/       dailies entire-dailies
```

## Task order

Task 1 first, alone. Then Tasks 2–7 in parallel, each in its own worktree. Then Tasks 8 and 9 in parallel. Then Task 10.

664	
665	- **One call per reel.** The free tier allows few generations per key per day, so all lines are sent as one text, joined by blank lines, prefixed with `Read as a calm, dry documentary narrator. Pause for a full second between paragraphs.\n\n`.
666	- **Gemini request.** `POST https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/<model>:generateContent`, header `x-goog-api-key`, body `{ contents: [{ parts: [{ text }] }], generationConfig: { responseModalities: ['AUDIO'], speechConfig: { voiceConfig: { prebuiltVoiceConfig: { voiceName } } } } }`. 667	- **Rotation.** Models are tried in order `gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview`, `gemini-3.8-flash-tts`, `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts`. HTTP 429 moves to the next key; when every key is exhausted for a model the next model is tried; when all fail `TtsQuotaError` is thrown. HTTP 5xx is retried twice with a 2 s wait.
668	- **`detectSilences`.** Runs `ffmpeg -i <wav> -af silencedetect=noise=<noiseDb>dB:d=<minSec> -f null -` (defaults -35 and 0.45) and parses `silence_start` / `silence_end` from stderr.
669	- **`alignLines`.** Drop silences touching the start or end of the audio. With `n` lines, `n - 1` boundaries are needed. The expected position of boundary `i` is `totalSec` times the cumulative share of characters up to line `i`. Each boundary takes the unused silence whose midpoint is nearest to its expected position and within 25% of `totalSec` of it; a boundary with no such silence uses the expected position. Line `i` runs from boundary `i - 1` to boundary `i` (0 and `totalSec` at the ends). The function never throws and always returns `n` contiguous, non-overlapping timings.
670	- **`estimateTimings`.** 15 characters per second, minimum 1.6 s per line, contiguous from zero.
671	- **`voiceLines`.** Uses a cached WAV under `outDir/cache/<sha256 of model list, voice and text>.wav` when present (zero calls). 63	
64	A **run** turns (repo, time window) into a reel. It is a fixed sequence of stages. Each stage reads the artifacts of earlier stages, writes one JSON artifact (plus files) and is idempotent.
65	
66	```
67	ingest -> edit -> verify -> script -> ground -> voice -> footage -> render -> review -> gate -> publish
68	                                ^                                              |
69	                                +---------- re-cut (at most 2 loops) ----------+
70	```
71	
72	The runner records every stage attempt in SQLite (status, attempt number, timings, artifact path, error). On process start it resumes unfinished runs from their last completed stage. Each stage has its own retry policy with backoff. `review` may send the run back to `script`, `voice` or `render`. `gate` ends in `needs_approval`, `blocked` (with reasons) or `approved`; `publish` only runs from `approved`.
73	
74	### Data model
75	
76	| Table | Holds |
77	|---|---|
78	| `repos` | URL, default branch, last checkpoint covered, stored preferences |
79	| `runs` | repo, window, status, cost so far, budget, trace id |
80	| `stages` | run, name, status, attempt, timings, artifact path, error |
81	| `claims` | run, session, quote, kind, verdict, evidence refs |
82	| `lines` | run, scene, narration text, evidence refs, audio path, duration |
83	| `reels` | run, video path, subtitles, poster, status (draft / approved / published) |
84	| `feedback` | repo, reel, free text, resulting preference |
85	| `events` | run, timestamp, stage, message (drives the live progress stream) |
86	
87	Artifacts (cloned repos, stage JSON, audio, frames, MP4) live under one data directory behind a small storage interface.
88	
89	## 4. Stages
90	
91	**4.1 Ingest (deterministic)**
92	Partial-clone the repo, fetch `refs/entire/*` and the legacy `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch if present. For each checkpoint read `metadata.json`, the per-session metadata, `prompt.txt` and the compact `transcript.jsonl`. Map checkpoints to commits through the `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. Select sessions inside the window. Redact secrets before anything else sees the text (key patterns, env assignments, high-entropy strings). Output: normalized `Session[]` with typed entries (user prompt, assistant text, tool call, tool result) and stable entry ids.
93	
94	Optional enrichments through the Entire CLI when it works on the clone: `entire checkpoint explain --json`, `entire graph diff|impact`, `entire dispatch --local`. Each is reported as `used` or `skipped`; nothing is invented when one is unavailable.
95	
96	**4.2 Edit (agent)**
97	Transcripts do not fit in context, so the editor navigates them with tools: `list_sessions`, `read_entries(session, range)`, `search_transcript(query)`, `get_diff(sha, path)`, `graph_impact(symbol)`. It returns at most six beats for the default 75-second target. A beat names its kind (feature, fix, decision, failure, recovery), the sessions and entry ranges it rests on and the commits involved.
98	
99	**4.3 Verify**
100	Extract the claims the coding agent made, then judge each one.
101	
102	Extraction: a small model reads assistant messages at turn ends and returns claims with the exact quote and the entry id. A claim is kept only if its quote is found in that entry (compared after collapsing whitespace and Markdown marks).
103	
104	| Claim kind | Evidence | Verdict rule |
105	|---|---|---|
106	| `tests_pass` | last test-runner call in the session before the claim, and its output | verified if it passed; contradicted if it failed; stale if code was edited after the last passing run; unverifiable if no run exists |
107	| `build_passes` | same for build, type-check and lint commands | same |
108	| `ran_command` | a matching tool call and its result | verified if it succeeded; contradicted if it errored; unverifiable if no matching call is recorded |
109	| `fixed_error` | the error text in an earlier tool result and a later run of the same command without it | unverifiable when no later run exists |
110	| `implemented` | the diff of the linked commits | a second model must quote the supporting hunk; the quote is validated against the diff |
111	
112	The first four are decided by deterministic parsers over the recorded tool results. Only `implemented` uses a model, from a different model family than the writer, and its quoted evidence is checked mechanically.
113	
114	**4.4 Script**
115	The writer produces a storyboard: ordered scenes with typed props and narration lines. The reel follows one arc: the problem (the human's request), the key decisions, the implementation, and the recorded validation. Each line carries evidence refs. Contradicted and stale claims become flag scenes. Unverifiable claims are either left out or stated as unverified.
116	
117	**4.5 Ground (gate, in code)**
118	For every line: evidence refs must resolve; every number in the sentence must appear in the facts computed for that scene; a second model must find the sentence entailed by the evidence. A failing line is rewritten up to twice, then dropped. A style lint (banned phrases, sentence length) runs here too. The on-screen text and narration are scanned again for secrets. The stage reports how many lines were dropped.
119	
120	**4.6 Voice**
121	Gemini text-to-speech per line, cached by content hash. Measured durations drive the timeline. On failure: retry with backoff, then an alternate voice, then a captions-only cut that is labelled as such.
122	
123	**4.7 Footage**
124	Scenes are rendered from data: title, quoted prompt, terminal replay, animated diff, stats, claim-versus-record flag, end card. Tier 3 adds a session timeline, the dependency-graph scene and a Playwright recording of the live app when the repo declares a URL.
125	
126	**4.8 Render**
127	Remotion composes the storyboard into 1080p30 MP4, an SRT file and a poster frame.
128	
129	**4.9 Review (agent)**
130	Deterministic checks first: total duration against target, silent gaps, black frames, per-scene text limits. Then frames from each scene go to a vision model with a fixed rubric (legibility, overflow, wrong or empty content). Findings map to fixes (shorten a line, change scene parameters, regenerate audio) and the run loops back, at most twice.
131	
132	**4.10 Gate (in code)**
133	All must hold: grounding passed, secret scan clean, review passed, cost within budget, human approval recorded. Failure of any condition blocks publishing; there is no override path in the worker.
134	
135	**4.11 Publish**
136	Mark the reel public, write the evidence page, draft a post for the human to send, and, on repositories the owner has authorised, comment the link on the pull request or commit.
137

--- name: timing description: Interpolation and timing in Remotion—prefer interpolate with Bézier easing; springs as a specialized option metadata: tags: easing, bezier, interpolation, spring, timing --- Drive motion with `interpolate()` over explicit frame range. To customize timing, use **`Easing.bezier`**. The four parameters are the same as CSS `cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`. A simple linear interpolation is done using the `interpolate` function. ```ts title="Going from 0 to 1 over 100 frames" import { interpolate } from "remotion"; const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 100], [0, 1]); ``` By default, the values are not clamped, so the value can go outside the range [0, 1]. Here is how they can be clamped: ```ts title="Going from 0 to 1 over 100 frames with extrapolation" const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 100], [0, 1], { extrapolateRight: "clamp", extrapolateLeft: "clamp", }); ``` ## Bézier easing Use `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)` inside the `interpolate` options object. The curve is identical in spirit to CSS animations and transitions, which helps when you are stealing timing from the web or from a designer’s spec. ```ts import { interpolate, Easing } from "remotion"; const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 60], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }); ``` ### Examples (copy-paste curves) **1. Crisp UI entrance (strong ease-out, no overshoot)** — slows nicely into the rest value; similar to many system “deceleration” curves. ```tsx const enter = interpolate(frame, [0, 45], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }); ``` **2. Editorial / slow fade (balanced ease-in-out)** — symmetric acceleration and deceleration over a hold-friendly move. ```tsx const progress = interpolate(frame, [0, 90], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.bezier(0.45, 0, 0.55, 1), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }); ``` **3. Playful overshoot (control point y > 1)** — a little past the target then settles; use sparingly for emphasis. ```tsx const pop = interpolate(frame, [0, 30], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }); ``` ## Preset easings (`Easing.in` / `Easing.out` / named curves) Easing can be added to the `interpolate` function without a custom cubic: ```ts import { interpolate, Easing } from "remotion"; const value1 = interpolate(frame, [0, 100], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }); ``` The default easing is `Easing.linear`. Convexities: - `Easing.in` — starting slow and accelerating - `Easing.out` — starting fast and slowing down - `Easing.inOut` Named curves (from most linear to most curved): - `Easing.quad` - `Easing.cubic` (good default when you do not need a custom cubic) - `Easing.sin` - `Easing.exp` - `Easing.circle` ### Easing direction for enter/exit animations Use `Easing.out` for enter animations (starts fast, decelerates into place) and `Easing.in` for exit animations (starts slow, accelerates away). This feels natural because elements arrive with momentum and leave with gravity. When you need a specific curve from design, prefer a single `Easing.bezier(...)` instead of stacking presets. ## Composing interpolations When multiple properties share the same timing (e.g. a slide-in panel and a video shift), avoid duplicating the full interpolation for each property. Instead, create a single normalized progress value (0 to 1) and derive each property from it: ```tsx const slideIn = interpolate( frame, [slideInStart, slideInStart + slideInDuration], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp", }, ); const slideOut = interpolate( frame, [slideOutStart, slideOutStart + slideOutDuration], [0, 1], { easing: Easing.in(Easing.cubic), extrapolateLeft: "clamp", extrapolateRight: "clamp" }, ); const progress = slideIn - slideOut; // Derive multiple properties from the same progress const overlayX = interpolate(progress, [0, 1], [100, 0]); const videoX = interpolate(progress, [0, 1], [0, -20]); const opacity = interpolate(progress, [0, 1], [0, 1]); ``` The key idea: separate **timing** (when and how fast) from **mapping** (what values to animate between). --- name: text-animations description: Typography and text animation patterns for Remotion. metadata: tags: typography, text, typewriter, highlighter ken --- ## Text animations Based on `useCurrentFrame()`, reduce the string character by character to create a typewriter effect. ## Typewriter Effect See [Typewriter](assets/text-animations-typewriter.tsx) for an advanced example with a blinking cursor and a pause after the first sentence. Always use string slicing for typewriter effects. Never use per-character opacity. ## Word Highlighting See [Word Highlight](assets/text-animations-word-highlight.tsx) for an example for how a word highlight is animated, like with a highlighter pen. --- name: sequencing description: Sequencing patterns for Remotion - delay, trim, limit duration of items metadata: tags: sequence, series, timing, delay, trim --- Use `` to delay when an element appears in the timeline. ```tsx import { Sequence } from "remotion"; export const Title = () => { const frame = useCurrentFrame(); const { fps } = useVideoConfig(); const opacity = interpolate(frame, [0, 2 * fps], [0, 1], { extrapolateRight: "clamp", extrapolateLeft: "clamp", easing: Easing.bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), }); return

If the items should not be wrapped, use the `layout` prop: ```tsx <Sequence layout="none"> <Title /> </Sequence> ``` ## Premounting This loads the component in the timeline before it is actually played. Always premount any `<Sequence>`! ```tsx <Sequence premountFor={1 * fps}> <Title /> </Sequence> ``` ## Series Use `<Series>` when elements should play one after another without overlap. ```tsx import { Series } from "remotion"; <Series> <Series.Sequence durationInFrames={45}> <Intro /> </Series.Sequence> <Series.Sequence durationInFrames={60}> <MainContent /> </Series.Sequence> <Series.Sequence durationInFrames={30}> <Outro /> </Series.Sequence> </Series>; ``` Same as with `<Sequence>`, the items will be wrapped in an absolute fill element by default when using `<Series.Sequence>`, unless the `layout` prop is set to `none`. ### Series with overlaps Use negative offset for overlapping sequences: ```tsx <Series> <Series.Sequence durationInFrames={60}> <SceneA /> </Series.Sequence> <Series.Sequence offset={-15} durationInFrames={60}> {/* Starts 15 frames before SceneA ends */} <SceneB /> </Series.Sequence> </Series> ``` ## Frame References Inside Sequences Inside a Sequence, `useCurrentFrame()` returns the local frame (starting from 0): ```tsx <Sequence from={60} durationInFrames={30}> <MyComponent /> {/* Inside MyComponent, useCurrentFrame() returns 0-29, not 60-89 */} </Sequence> ``` ## Nested Sequences Sequences can be nested for complex timing: ```tsx <Sequence from={0} durationInFrames={120}> <Background /> <Sequence from={15} durationInFrames={90} layout="none"> <Title /> </Sequence> <Sequence from={45} durationInFrames={60} layout="none"> <Subtitle /> </Sequence> </Sequence> ``` ## Nesting compositions within another To add a composition within another composition, you can use the `<Sequence>` component with a `width` and `height` prop to specify the size of the composition. ```tsx <AbsoluteFill> <Sequence width={COMPOSITION_WIDTH} height={COMPOSITION_HEIGHT}> <CompositionComponent /> </Sequence> </AbsoluteFill> ``` Shell cwd was reset to /Users/yehor/Desktop/projects/neathack-wt/6-reel

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: every interface produced by Tasks 2–7.
- Produces:
```ts
export interface StageDeps { client: ModelClient; meter: CostMeter; tts: TtsProvider | null; voice: string }
export function buildStages(deps: StageDeps): Stage[]     // ingest, edit, verify, script, ground, voice, render, review?, gate
export interface EditArtifact { beats: Beat[] }
export interface VerifyArtifact { claims: Claim[]; counts: Record<Verdict, number> }
export interface GroundArtifact { storyboard: Storyboard; dropped: { lineId: string; reasons: string[] }[]; kept: number }
export interface VoiceArtifact { mode: 'voiced' | 'captions'; audioPath: string | null; timings: LineTiming[]; calls: number }
export interface GateArtifact { checks: { name: string; pass: boolean; reasons: string[] }[] }
```
`buildStages` returns the stages without `review`; Task 9 exports `reviewStage(deps)` and Task 10 inserts it before `gate`.

Stage behaviour:

- **ingest.** Calls `ingest()`. `NoCheckpointsError` or an empty session list returns `final: { status: 'blocked', reason: 'no agent sessions found in this window' }`.
- **edit.** `runAgent` with role `editor` and tools over the ingest artifact:
  - `list_sessions()` → id, agent, model, start, end, entry count, commits, first user prompt cut to 200 characters.
  - `read_entries({ sessionId, from, to })` → at most 40 entries, each text cut to 600 characters.
  - `search_transcript({ query })` → up to 20 matching entries with ids.
  - `get_diff({ sha })` → paths with added and removed counts; `get_patch({ sha, path })` → the patch.

  Output schema `{ beats: Beat[] }`, at most six. After parsing, a beat is dropped if any range names an unknown session or indexes outside it. Zero beats left is an error (the runner retries).
- **verify.** For each session, the extractor (`completeJson`, role `extractor`) receives the assistant entries that end a turn (the last assistant text before each user entry and the final one), each as `{ entryId, text }`, in batches of 30. It returns `{ claims: [{ entryId, quote, kind, subject? }] }`. Claims whose quote fails `quoteMatches` are dropped. `verifyClaims` judges the four deterministic kinds. Each `implemented` claim goes to the judge (role `judge`) with the patches of the session's commits; the judge returns `{ supported: boolean, path?: string, quote?: string }`. It is `verified` only if `supported` and the quote is found in that patch; `supported: false` gives `unverifiable`, never `contradicted`.
- **script.** Code builds the frame, the model writes only narration.
  - Code creates the title scene, one flag scene per `contradicted` or `stale` claim (at most three, newest first) and the end scene. A flag scene's narration is a template, not model text: `The agent wrote: "<quote cut to 120 characters>".` plus, by reason, `The last test run before that message had failed.` / `Code was edited after the last passing run.` / the rule's `reason`. The quote and the reality sentence are two separate lines. Their evidence is the claim's evidence.
  - The writer (role `writer`) receives the beats, the verified claims, the facts and the entries each beat points to, and returns spoken scenes of types `prompt`, `terminal`, `diff`, `stats` with one-sentence lines that each cite evidence. `ctx.feedback`, when set, is appended to the prompt.
  - The writer is told to follow one arc: the problem (a `prompt` scene quoting the human's request), the key decisions, the implementation (`diff`), the recorded validation (`terminal` with the commands that were actually run), then `stats`.
  - The storyboard is assembled as title, writer scenes in that arc with each flag scene placed after the validation scene of its session, end. Target 75 s.
- **ground.** For every line run `checkLine`. A passing line then goes to the entailment check (role `judge`): given the line and the text of its evidence, reply `{ entailed: boolean }`. A failing line is rewritten by the writer with the reasons, at most twice, then dropped. A scene left with no lines is removed. Flag-scene template lines skip the model check and the style lint (`skipStyle`), but their evidence refs must still resolve. If fewer than two spoken scenes remain the stage loops back to `script` with the reasons. The whole stage runs inside `guard('grounding', …)`.
- **voice.** `voiceLines` over all lines in order with `maxCalls = run.budget.maxTtsCalls`; `tts === null` gives captions mode.
- **render.** `renderReel` into `<runDir>/reel`.
- **gate.** Inside `guard('publish_gate', …)` evaluate and record: grounding (no line without evidence in the final storyboard), secrets (`redact` over every on-screen string and line reports zero hits), cost (`meter.total() <= run.budget.maxCostPerReelUsd`), review (no high-severity finding in the review artifact; when no review stage ran, `ctx.read('review')` throws and the check is recorded as passed with the reason `review skipped`). Any failure returns `final: { status: 'blocked', reason: <failed check names> }`. All passing returns `final: { status: 'needs_approval', reason: 'awaiting human approval' }`.

After every stage that used the model, `addCost(db, run.id, delta)` records the meter's increase.
